pedagogy.summary: Adding up to four two-digit numbers is where the properties of operations become a practical tool: because addition is commutative and associative, children may reorder and regroup the addends to make the work easier — hunting for pairs that make a multiple of ten, then partitioning the rest into tens and ones. The efficiency insight (look before you leap) matters as much as accuracy; the composing of several tens at once is the new demand over two-addend work.
bestPractices: Teach 'look for pairs that make ten (or a multiple of ten)' before adding — reorder using commutativity/associativity (extends adding three one-digit numbers)
Partition all addends into tens and ones, sum the tens, sum the ones, then recombine — composing as many tens/hundreds as needed
Encourage jottings to keep track when combining many ones, to prevent accumulation slips
Discuss which grouping was smartest and why, so the properties are used deliberately not accidentally
Use manipulatives/ten-frames so 'making a ten' from a pair is seen, then move to numbers
keyRepresentations: Ten-frames / bead strings (spotting pairs that make ten)
Draggable number cards (reorder addends to pair)
Part-whole / column jottings (tens together, ones together)
commonMisconceptions: Adding strictly left-to-right and missing pairs that make ten (not using commutativity to simplify)
Losing track when combining many ones, or forgetting to compose more than one ten (ones sum to 23, only one ten carried)
Believing the addends must be added in the given order (no reordering allowed)
Miscounting during a long running total

learn.summary: Children add up to four two-digit numbers by using the commutative and associative properties as a practical tool: reorder and regroup addends to find pairs that make a multiple of ten, then partition the rest into tens and ones, sum each, and recombine. The 'look before you leap' efficiency insight matters alongside accuracy, and composing several tens at once is the new demand over two-addend work. The strongest version lets the child physically reorder addends and see pairs combine into round numbers; recognition tasks and static ringed examples are useful rehearsal and reference, but because they do not themselves require the child to reorder addends they check the strategy more than they elicit the independent habit of looking for pairs first.

activities.title: Snap the pairs that make a tidy number
feedback: If the child adds left-to-right without scanning, don't reteach addition: ask 'before you start, can you see any two that make a tidy number?' and let them re-experience the shortcut.
When two cards combine into a round number (e.g. 15 and 25 becoming 40), name it: 'those two made exactly 40, so now you only have round numbers left.'

If the child insists the numbers must stay in the written order, demonstrate with counters that the total is the same in any order, and connect it to adding three one-digit numbers where pairing to ten was allowed.

OPTIONAL: on a screen version, cards whose sum is a multiple of ten can snap into a labelled '40' or '20' block, remaining tens and ones can auto-partition and recombine to show the composed tens, and a side-by-side 'left-to-right vs paired' race can make the efficiency gain visible. These are illustrative ways to make the mechanism concrete, not required features.
activities.rationale: Physically reordering and watching pairs fuse into round numbers rewards spotting the number bond and makes the commutative/associative strategy deliberate rather than accidental. Reordering to check and simplify is the curriculum route by which these properties are established at this stage.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils add three one-digit numbers and, building on this, add numbers including combining several addends; adding numbers in a different order is used to check and establishes commutativity and associativity.
Choosing an efficient order of addition (identifying two addends that make ten) uses the associative and commutative laws; children need not use the formal terms at this stage.
learnerActions: Take four addends to add, e.g. 15, 8, 25, and 12, arranged as cards that can be physically moved (paper cards, counters on a tray, or draggable on-screen tiles).
Before adding anything, scan the four numbers and decide which two, placed together, would make a multiple of ten.
Pair 15 with 25 to make 40, and 8 with 12 to make 20, then add the two round numbers: 40 + 20 = 60.
Repeat with 24, 17, 6, 13 (24+6=30 and 17+13=30, giving 60) and say aloud which pair you spotted first and why.
Try one example by adding strictly left-to-right, then again by pairing first, and compare how much easier the paired route felt.
activities.intendedInsight: Because addition can be done in any order and grouping, reordering to make pairs that total a multiple of ten turns a fearsome four-number sum into an easy sum of round numbers. The properties of operations are a lever, not an abstraction.

activities.title: Partition into tens and ones, and compose the tens carefully
feedback: If the answer is off by exactly ten, the child likely composed one ten from the ones and dropped a second: have them pool all the ones again and count how many full tens they can make.
Encourage jottings to track the running total of ones so slips don't accumulate.
If the tens are right but the total drifts, slow the recombination step and check how many tens came out of the ones.
activities.rationale: Composing several tens at once is the genuinely new demand of four-addend work; pooling all ones before exchanging and making the exchange visible with base-ten targets the specific 'dropped a composed ten' error.
learnerActions: Take all four addends and split each into its tens and its ones: for 15, 8, 25, 12 the tens are 10, 0, 20, 10 (the single-digit 8 has no tens) and the ones are 5, 8, 5, 2.
Add all the tens together (10 + 0 + 20 + 10 = 40), then pool ALL the ones together before exchanging.

From the pooled ones, exchange every full ten you can: here 5 + 8 + 5 + 2 = 20, which makes two tens and no leftover ones; if the ones had totalled 23 you would make two tens (not one) and keep 3 ones.
Recombine the composed tens with the tens you already had (40 + 20 = 60) and check it matches the paired-up method.
Use base-ten blocks or ten-frames so that making more than one ten from the ones is something you can see, not just carry in your head.
activities.intendedInsight: When many ones are combined they can compose more than one ten. Pooling all the ones and exchanging every full ten before recombining is a reliable way to make sure no composed ten is lost. If a composed ten is dropped, the answer comes out ten too small, or more than ten too small if several tens are dropped.

activities.title: Explain and defend the smartest grouping
feedback: If the child can solve but can't explain, ask them to point to the pair that made a round number and say the new, simpler sum it created.
Accept informal language; the formal terms 'commutative' and 'associative' are not required at this stage.
If the child spots pairs only when prompted, praise the find and ask them to scan unprompted on the next sum to build the habit.
activities.rationale: Articulating the strategy distinguishes a child using the properties deliberately from one who adds accurately but never looks for simplifying pairs; reasoning about reordering is how the curriculum establishes commutativity and associativity.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils add three one-digit numbers and, building on this, add numbers including combining several addends; adding numbers in a different order is used to check and establishes commutativity and associativity.
Choosing an efficient order of addition (identifying two addends that make ten) uses the associative and commutative laws; children need not use the formal terms at this stage.
learnerActions: After solving a four-addend sum, say which two numbers you added first and why that order made the work easier.
Answer 'you added them in a different order than they're written — does that change the answer, and how do you know?'
Given 19 + 4 + 1 + 6, decide which you would add first and justify it (19 + 1 makes 20, then + 4 + 6 reaches 30).
Pick a sum where no neat pair exists and explain what you do then (partition into tens and ones).
activities.intendedInsight: Explaining the chosen grouping makes the properties a conscious, reusable strategy and shows that reordering never changes the total.

constraints: Prerequisite: pairing numbers to make ten (as in adding three one-digit numbers) and exchanging ten ones for a ten; revisit these if a child insists order is fixed or loses a composed ten.

Recognition-style tasks (matching pairs that make ten, choosing the smartest first step, filling blanks in running totals) rehearse and check the strategy and can catch left-to-right grinding, but because they do not require the child to reorder the addends themselves they do not on their own elicit the independent habit of looking for pairs first; pair them with tasks where the child reorders the addends.
A static worked example with the pairs ringed is useful reference but does not let the child try reordering; use it alongside, not instead of, hands-on regrouping.
Manipulatives (ten-frames, bead strings, base-ten blocks) should make 'making a ten' and composing several tens visible before moving to numbers alone.
Keep sums engineered so tidy pairs exist when teaching the strategy, but also include a sum with no neat pair so the child learns the fallback of partitioning into tens and ones.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched and the listed source claims retain their original verification status (one marked verified, one not). Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The original 'worked correct answer' example lists ones such as 5+8+5+2=20 for the first sum (composing two tens), consistent with the 'ones can exceed ten' point; retained as-is.

The original row asserted '3D adds nothing' and 'talk cannot supply the manipulation-and-feedback practice the strategy needs'. These comparative/necessity claims are not established by the sources and have been softened: spoken discussion is used productively in the explain/defend activity, and the hands-on reordering is proposed on its affordances (physical regrouping and feedback) rather than as the only possible medium.

Comparative efficacy wording in the summary was tightened to the observable limit that recognition/static tasks do not require the child to reorder; no claim of tested superiority of any medium is made.

probeDeeper: Before adding, did any two of these numbers jump out as making a tidy total? Which?
You added them in a different order than they're written — does that change the answer? How do you know?
Your ones added up to more than ten — how many tens did you make from them?
If I gave you 19 + 4 + 1 + 6, which would you add first, and why?
assess.correctAnswer: 60 and 60. Efficiently: 15+25=40 and 8+12=20 → 60; 24+6=30 and 17+13=30 → 60. Alternatively partition all into tens and ones (tens 10+20+... , ones summed and composed). Both reach 60; the strategy question is whether pairs are spotted.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds strictly left-to-right, never scanning for pairs that make ten — '15 and 8 is 23, and 25 is 48…'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach addition; prompt 'before you start, can you see any two that make a tidy number?' and let them re-experience the shortcut. Build the looking-first habit.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The child works in given order with no pause to look for bonds; the skill of pairing is available but not deployed

errorPatterns.pattern: Loses a composed ten when combining many ones — ones total 23 but only one ten is carried, or the running total drifts
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have the child pool ALL the ones first and exchange as many tens as possible before recombining; use base-ten so multiple composed tens are visible.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The tens are right but the answer is off by ten; the child composed one ten from the ones and dropped the second

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes the numbers must be added in the order written — resists reordering
errorPatterns.nextMove: Demonstrate with counters that the total is the same in any order; connect to adding three one-digit numbers where pairing to ten was allowed.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When invited to reorder, the child says you can't, or that it would change the answer

responseLevels.gap: Adds left-to-right, drops composed tens, or insists order is fixed; answers unreliable and slow.
responseLevels.full: Scans for pairs making multiples of ten, reorders confidently using the properties, composes multiple tens correctly, and explains why the chosen grouping was efficient.
responseLevels.partial: Adds accurately by partitioning but doesn't yet look for pairs to simplify, or spots pairs only when prompted.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set two calculations and watch how the child tackles each, thinking aloud: 15 + 8 + 25 + 12, then 24 + 17 + 6 + 13. Notice whether they look for pairs that make a multiple of ten before adding, and how they combine the ones.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Both sums are engineered so pairs make tidy multiples of ten. A child who uses commutativity spots the pairs and finishes quickly and accurately; a child who grinds left-to-right is slower and far more likely to slip when the running total's ones exceed ten. Watching the ORDER they add in exposes whether the properties are a live tool.
